articles.title: Australia 56-17 Japan: Wallabies seal series as 1,000th cap recipient scores on debut
articles.summary: Australia wrap up two-Test series win with eight-try victory over Eddie Jones’ Japan; Japan remain winless against Wallabies in nine Tests, stretching back to 1975; watch the entire South Africa vs New Zealand Test series live on Sky Sports from August 22
articles.body:
Prop Taniela Tupou scored a double before his replacement, De Lutiis, scored on debut to mark becoming the 1,000th Wallaby with his first international try.

Six of Australia's eight tries were scored by front-row forwards, with hooker Josh Nasser, loosehead Angus Bell and replacement hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa all getting on the scoresheet.

Flanker Charlie Cale and skipper Harry Wilson chipped in with late scores, while scrum-half Ryan Lonergan and replacement fly-half Ben Donaldson combined to kick all eight conversions.

Japan scored first-half tries through Harry Hockings, Naoto Saito and Dylan Riley but were kept pointless after the break as their losing streak against Australia, which dates back to 1975, extended to nine Tests.

Australia took an early lead twice via tries from Josh Nasser and Tupou, but Saito and Ryunosuke Ito supplied quick ball to regularly expose holes in the Wallabies defence as Japan rallied both times.

Lock Hockings charged down a poor attempted exit from Lonergan at the base of a ruck and dived on the ball in goal, while Saito took a quick-tap penalty and darted over from close range.

Japan took the lead in the 33rd minute through Australian-born Dylan Riley, who beat two tackles and reached over for a try, but Australia hit back before the break via a line-out move from which Tupou crashed over.

De Lutiis came on in the 50th minute to replace veteran prop Tupou, who barged over for two first-half tries, and was on the shoulder of Angus Bell a minute later as his fellow front-rower scored to give Australia a 26-17 lead.

De Lutiis scored himself in the 58th minute, backing up in support at the perfect time after an Australian attacking raid that started with fly-half Carter Gordon breaking the defensive line and running 30 metres towards the right corner flag.

That try and a conversion from scrum-half Ryan Lonergan, his fifth, gave Australia an 18-point cushion with 20 minutes remaining after a tightly contested first half in which Japan's surprising line speed in defence and enterprising, relentless attack unsettled the Wallabies.

Three late tries helped the Wallabies turn a 21-17 half-time lead into a 39-point victory, giving the Australians a three-match winning streak for the first time since 2024.

The Wallabies beat Italy last month in the Nations Championship in Joe Schmidt's last match as head coach, before a 35-32 win over Japan in Osaka last weekend in Les Kiss' first game in charge.

articles.summary: South Africa and New Zealand renew rugby's 'Greatest Rivalry' in the first match of their four Test series at Ellis Park this Saturday; watch South Africa vs New Zealand live on Sky Sports Action on Saturday from 4.10pm
articles.body:
Springboks head coach Rassie Erasmus named the inexperienced Paul de Villiers in his matchday squad ahead of Kolisi, who has been nursing a hamstring injury sustained in their 17-10 victory over Argentina on August 8.

With three further Tests against the All Blacks to come in Cape Town, Johannesburg and Baltimore, USA, Kolisi has not been risked.

"Siya trained well with us this week, and although we could have selected him for this clash, we thought it would be best to select Paul," Erasmus said.

"We are playing four Tests against the All Blacks and Paul has been playing well, so we are excited to give him a chance this weekend in what will be his first Test match against New Zealand, while taking a precautionary approach to Siya's return.

"We have a solid group of players, and each one of them deserves their place in the squad, so we will approach team selection week by week."

Centre Damian de Allende will earn his 100th Test cap at Ellis Park, becoming the 10th player in South African rugby history to reach the century landmark.

Fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu and lock Eben Etzebeth are the only players to retain their starting positions from the victory in Buenos Aires.

Prop Ox Nche, meanwhile, starts for the first time since July's Nations Championship victory over England.

South Africa have won five of their last six Tests against New Zealand, including inflicting a record 43-10 defeat on their great rivals in Wellington last September.

"They are a quality team and they're very well coached, so we are preparing for an 80-minute grind," Erasmus added.

"They have a well-rounded squad with physical forwards and an exciting backline, so we have to be sharp and accurate in our execution from the outset.

"Many of the matches between the sides have come down to the wire, so it's important that we use the chances we create and ensure that our discipline is on point.

Captain Savea, scrum-half Roigard and record try-scoring wing Jordan will make their first appearances of this summer's tour of South Africa, while full-back Damian McKenzie returns after injuring his ankle in the warm-up victory over the Sharks in Durban.

Head coach Dave Rennie has blended experience with youth, with 110-cap duo Savea and Codie Taylor facing the Springboks for the 18th and 17th time respectively, while Anton Segner and Josh Moorby will face South Africa for the first time.

"After all the build-up and anticipation, our whole touring squad is excited to get this first Test underway," Rennie said.

articles.title: South Africa vs New Zealand live on Sky Sports: The history of 'rugby's greatest rivalry' ahead of four-Test series
articles.summary: We chronicle rugby rivalry between All Blacks and Springboks from 1921-2026: South Africa's apartheid era, contentious World Cup finals, respective periods on top; watch New Zealand's tour of South Africa live on Sky Sports+, with first Test on Saturday August 22 (4.10pm)
articles.body:
It's been advertised in New Zealand and South Africa as "Rugby's Greatest Rivalry Tour." A series of games to celebrate over a century of contests between the two most successful nations the sport has seen.

The All Blacks have already played and beaten the Stormers, Sharks and Bulls so far, and face the Springboks in Tests on August 22, August 29, September 5 and September 12.

So, what is the history between the two? And what have been the flashpoints and major moments over the decades? We take a look...

New Zealand and South Africa first met on August 13, 1921 in Carisbrook, Dunedin as part of South Africa's three-Test tour, with the All Blacks coming out with a 13-5 victory.

South Africa won a week later at Eden Park 9-5, with the third Test a 0-0 draw in Wellington to see the series end 1-1. And so set in motion a rugby rivalry which has endured right at the apex of the sport.

That first match included, there have been some 110 Test meetings, the All Blacks winning 63, South Africa 43 and four draws.

There have been 54 Tests played in South Africa, with the hosts winning 28, New Zealand 25 and one draw, while 48 Tests in New Zealand have seen the All Blacks win 34, Springboks 11 and three draws.

At Rugby World Cups, South Africa have beaten New Zealand in two dramatic finals (1995, 2023), and in one third-place playoff (1999), while New Zealand have beaten South Africa in the 2015 semi-finals, 2003 quarter-finals and 2023 pool stages.

After that original 1921 tour, the next time the sides met came in 1927 when New Zealand toured South Africa and again, the series finished in a captivating draw: 2-2 this time with wins for the Boks in Durban and Port Elizabeth, and wins for the All Blacks in Johannesburg and Cape Town.

South Africa won the next two series between the sides, touring New Zealand in 1937 and winning 2-1, while hosting the All Blacks in 1949 and winning 4-0.

In 1956, New Zealand get their own back as they clinched a 3-1 home series success over the Springboks, though 1960 saw South Africa back to winning ways via a 2-1 series win back on home soil.

South Africa's apartheid era, worldwide sporting ban and protests

Between 1948 and 1994, though, South Africa enforced apartheid, the institutionalised racial segregation and white minority rule.

As part of this shameful system, South Africa refused to allow people of different races to play sport together, with officials requesting Māori players not be involved in series between the nations. New Zealand agreed and excluded some of their finest players from several tours, with the first major public protests coming during that 1960 tour to South Africa.

By 1964, South Africa as a sporting nation were barred from participating at the Tokyo Olympic Games, and in 1970 they were formally expelled from the International Olympic Committee. They were excluded from international tennis and the Davis Cup the same year.

Throughout the rest of the 1970s, widespread cancellations and bans for South Africa in international sport continued, but rugby proved one of the last to take action.

Indeed, 1965 saw South Africa tour New Zealand with the All Blacks winning three Tests to one, before the Halt All Racist Tours protest group was established in New Zealand in 1969 to oppose continued tours to and from South Africa.

The All Blacks toured South Africa in 1970 in any case, losing 3-1 to the Springboks, and though a 1973 tour to New Zealand was cancelled amid a climate of South Africa's worldwide sporting expulsion, series between the nations still took place in 1976 and 1981 - South Africa winning the former at home 3-1, and New Zealand the latter series 2-1 which was dogged by protests and worldwide condemnation.

Indeed, during that 1981 tour two games were cancelled. One in Hamilton saw 200 protestors rip down a chain fence, sprinkle nails all over the pitch and stage a sit-in on the halfway line, while a match against South Canterbury at Timaru was cancelled because the authorities said they would not be able to control demonstrations there.

During the final Test of the tour, an aircraft continually flew overhead the pitch and dropped flour bombs, flares and leaflets in protest. All Blacks prop Gary Knight was temporarily stunned by a flour bomb.

Eventually, the planned 1985 series between the two was cancelled in line with South Africa's wider sporting ban, with a legal ruling in New Zealand determining it would be "incompatible with the NZRFU's legally stated purpose of fostering and encouragement of the game of rugby."

The Springboks were barred from rugby's first two World Cups in 1987 and 1991, while a 1986 British and Irish Lions tour was also cancelled.

After the 1985 series between South Africa and New Zealand was cancelled, a 'rebel tour' which was not government-sanctioned was organised, and a team travelled in 1986 called New Zealand Cavaliers. The Kiwi players involved received condemnation, were banned for several Tests after the tour and some never played for New Zealand again.

South Africa's return to international sport and contentious World Cup glory

Upon the end of the apartheid regime, South Africa organised a Test against the All Blacks in 1992 for their first encounter since being welcomed back to international sport, and even went on to surprisingly win it 27-24 at Ellis Park.

With the released Nelson Mandela inaugurated as president in 1994, he encouraged all South Africans to back the previously hated Springboks.

In 1994, South Africa toured New Zealand for the first time in nearly 20 years, losing two Tests and drawing one, with South Africa then hosting the 1995 Rugby World Cup.

Ranked ninth in the world after their lengthy period of sporting exile, South Africa shocked many by progressing to the final where Jonah Lomu and the All Blacks awaited.

A fairytale 15-12 World Cup final victory over New Zealand at Ellis Park followed, but was there foul play involved?

The All Blacks had outscored their opponents 315-104 en route to the final, and were heavy, heavy favourites, yet they failed to score a single try in a contest that went through extra- time. How?

For many, the reason lies with the fact that a hefty proportion of the New Zealand team were struck down by illness or food poisoning on the cusp of the final.

For All Blacks head coach at the time, Laurie Mains, the culprit was a disappearing waitress named 'Suzie' - a conspiracy theory that was never proven, though Mains even hired a private investigator after the final. Team doctor Mike Bowen has also always insisted the All Blacks were poisoned, as has South African security guard Rory Steyn.

What is indisputable is that a large majority of the All Blacks squad were struck down with violent illness in the days before a World Cup final against the Springboks in South Africa.

New Zealand's 'Incomparables' and period of dominance

A little over a year after that World Cup final, the All Blacks toured South Africa in August 1996 set on revenge.

They had already beaten the Springboks home and away during the inaugural 1996 Tri-Nations, clinching the title, but a three-Test tour in South Africa against the world champions was built up as the next major challenge.

In New Zealand, that side are now known as 'The Incomparables,' as they played some magnificent rugby to launch rugby's era of professionalism, winning the first Test 23-19 in Durban, and then the second Test 33-26 at Loftus Versfeld in Pretoria, clinching the series with a Test to spare.

South Africa won that third Test, but it mattered little as the All Blacks kicked on to win 13 of the next 17 contests - going unbeaten against the Boks between 2001 and July 2004. Tri-Nations titles followed in 1997, 1999, 2002 and 2003.

The Springboks landed Tri-Nations titles in 2004 and 2009, but outside of those years, New Zealand firmly established themselves as the premier nation on the globe.

The All Blacks won Tri-Nations titles four years in a row between 2005 and 2008, again in 2010, then three more years in a row between 2011 and 2013, and three more years in a row again between 2016 and 2018. They also lifted Rugby World Cup titles in 2011 and 2015 - the latter with a side many consider the greatest ever.

They were caught by France at the 2007 World Cup despite being huge favourites, as South Africa went on to lift their second Webb Ellis Trophy, but the Boks failed to clinch silverware in any form between 2009 and 2019.

September 16, 2017 proved one of South Africa's darkest rugby days, when they travelled to Albany and were defeated 57-0 by the All Blacks.

They were beaten by Ireland 38-3 in Dublin two months later, losing to Wales in Cardiff the same Test window. Such form followed a 2016 in which the Springboks were soundly beaten by England and Wales, lost to Italy for the first time, were beaten by Argentina and Australia, lost to Ireland at home and went down 57-15 to the All Blacks.

Enough was enough, and so heralded the era of Rassie Erasmus.

The controversial, unusual rugby head coach of the Springboks totally turned around South Africa's fortunes.

By September 2018, a rejuvenated, confident side travelled to New Zealand and picked up a shock 36-34 victory in Wellington - a first win on Kiwi soil since 2009.

A little over a year later, South Africa became world champions for the third time, clinching World Cup glory vs England in the final in Japan - Eddie Jones' side having dealt with the All Blacks in the semi-finals, after the latter had beaten South Africa during the pool stages.

Since that tournament, in 11 Tests between South Africa and New Zealand, the Springboks have won seven of them, winning Rugby Championship crowns in 2024 and 2025, and the 2023 Rugby World Cup final - albeit the latter victory came in fortunate fashion, it must be said, against a 14-player All Blacks side who probably deserved victory.

If the 2023 South Africa side was strong, the current one is likely even better, with greater depth, while the All Blacks are looking to rebuild again under Dave Rennie, with Scott Robertson having been sacked.

"With eight matches in six weeks, including a four-Test series against the Springboks, this would have to be the toughest tour in rugby," Rennie said.

"It will be an intense seven weeks of touring but an excellent opportunity for us to pit ourselves against the current benchmark team in world rugby, and to build connections with each other in a way that only a tour of this scale can do."

articles.title: South Africa vs New Zealand: All Blacks emerge worthy winners as they outscore Springboks in first Test upset
articles.summary: South Africa lose their first game at home since August 16 2025 after a huge second half from New Zealand sees them pull away from the Springboks to claim a 33–16 victory at Ellis Park and take the opening Test of the series
articles.body:
The Boks led 13-12 at half-time, but New Zealand took over in the second half to close it out and end South Africa's unbeaten streak.

The All Blacks had ​been underdogs going into the first international of their eight-match tour ​but took full ⁠advantage of the ⁠home side's numerous handling errors and ill discipline ‌for a statement victory that ended a 12-match winning streak for ‌the Springboks and will rock the confidence of the world champions.

"I'm incredibly proud, the score might be convincing but there was nothing in it and it ​was an absolute arm wrestle," said winning coach Dave Rennie.

"We defended and defended and we were clinical when we got our ⁠opportunities. It's a great result for us,"

Will Jordan extended his run as ⁠New Zealand's record try ​scorer with two tries that ​bookended scores from Josh ​Moorby, Fabian Holland and Luke ⁠Jacobson.

Ruben Love kicked over four conversions.

South Africa's try came ⁠from Andre Esterhuizen with ​three penalties and a conversion ​from Cheslin Kolbe but they lost their discipline towards the end, after multiple turnovers, and finished with 13 players as Marco van Staden and Cobus Reinach were sent to the ‌sin bin in the final 10 minutes.

"In hindsight there were two or three big moments where we let the game get away from us because New Zealand forced us into ‌errors by being intense and sharp," said coach Rassie ​Erasmus.

The series moves to sea level in Cape Town next Saturday and New Zealand are now the surprising front-runner in the first full series between the teams in 30 years.

articles.title: South Africa v New Zealand: Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu drops to bench
articles.summary: Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu pays for an indifferent showing in South Africa's series opener against New Zealand, as the fly-half drops to the Springbok bench.
articles.body:
Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu has paid the price for an indifferent showing in South Africa's defeat by New Zealand, with the fly-half dropping to the bench for Saturday's rematch in Cape Town.

The All Blacks, revitalised under new coach Dave Rennie, ran out 33-16 winners in the series opener in Johannesburg.

Feinberg-Mngomezulu was turned over five times in possession and occasionally exposed in defence, before he shifted to full-back for the Springboks in the second half of Saturday's first Test.

South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus has recalled 32-year-old double Rugby World Cup winner Handre Pollard at 10, while injuries to Cheslin Kolbe and Grant Williams have brought Ethan Hooker and Cobus Reinach into the starting line-up at wing and scrum-half respectively.

Siya Kolisi may return to the back row after recovering from a hamstring injury, but Erasmus has also named Paul de Villiers as a back-up at blindside flanker in case Kolisi is not ready.

Thirty-nine year-old Deon Fourie, who came off the bench to play 77 minutes of the Springboks' 2023 Rugby World Cup final win over New Zealand, could win his first cap since that occasion after being named among the replacements.

"There were a handful of positives and negatives last week, but the main thing that let us down was that we created so many chances, but mistakes at crucial times cost us," said Erasmus.

"We'll put in a lot of work this week to ensure that we are sharp in that regard this weekend because if we had used even some of those chances, the result could have been completely different."

South Africa side to face New Zealand: Willemse; Arendse, Kriel, De Allende, Hooker; Pollard, Reinach; Nche, Marx, Louw, Etzebeth, Nortje, Kolisi/De Villiers, PS du Toit, Wiese.

Replacements: Fourie, Steenekamp, T du Toit, De Jager, Esterhuizen, Hanekom, Van den Berg, Feinberg-Mngomezulu.

'I'm ready' - Mo'unga fired up for All Blacks return

New Zealand may be tempted to give Richie Mo'unga an immediate Test return as they chase a 2-0 lead in the four-match series that has been marketed as 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry'.

The 32-year-old was first-choice stand-off during their 2023 Rugby World Cup campaign, but he has been ineligible for selection while playing his club rugby in Japan since.

However, his signing for Canterbury and the Crusaders, along with an injury to Billy Proctor, has paved the way for his comeback.

Mo'unga will start at 10 in Tuesday's match against Johannesburg-based provincial side the Lions.

Mo'unga, who says his determination to return to Tests was fuelled by watching a Six Nations match while in a Japanese karaoke bar last year, is confident he can produce the form that earned him a spot in World Rugby's team of 2023.

"I'm competitive; I want to be the best," he said. "I know that there's a process to that, and at this point in time, the process looks a bit different around preparing someone else [All Blacks' current first-choice fly-half Ruben Love] to be the best.

"I'm really competitive, but I'm also a team man. Whoever gets the role, gets the role, and if it's not me, I'll do anything I can to help them succeed.

"This game was always coming for me. There was always going to be a return. I wasn't sure when it was, but mentally I've prepared for my return in the black jersey, and I'm ready."

New Zealand side to face Lions: B Barrett; Fineanganofo, Ioane, Tavatavanawai, Narawa; Mo'unga, Hotham; Lauaki, Taukei'aho, Tosi, Darry, Tuipulotu, Sititi, Blackadder, Ta'eiloa.

Replacements: Slater, Tu'ungafasi, Ma'u, Hannah, Lakai, Preston, Jacomb, Lienert-Brown.

articles.title: South Africa vs New Zealand: Siya Kolisi, Handre Pollard return as Springboks look to level Test series in Cape Town
articles.summary: Siya Kolisi, Handre Pollard, Cobus Reinach and Ethan Hooker drafted into much-changed Springboks XV ahead of Saturday's must-win second Test against the All Blacks; watch South Africa vs New Zealand live from 4.55pm on Sky Sports Action and Sky Sports +
articles.body:
The back-to-back reigning world champions surrendered top spot in the rankings to the All Blacks after Saturday's shock 33-16 defeat, their heaviest home loss to New Zealand.

The Springboks travel to Cape Town for the second instalment in the first four-Test series between the two sides in 50 years knowing only a victory will keep their hopes of winning alive.

Coach Rassie Erasmus has responded defeat in Johannesburg by making four changes to his starting XV and bringing five fresh faces onto the replacements bench.

Kolisi will start at flanker providing the hamstring issue which ruled him out of the first Test doesn't resurface during training. If he remains unfit, Paul de Villiers will retain his position at No 7.

The Springboks coach highlighted Kolisi's value at the breakdown and in organising South Africa's defensive structure alongside Pieter-Steph du Toit, areas he felt were lacking in the first Test.

"Paul played well on Saturday and there's no reason why we should keep him out, but Siya is our captain," Erasmus said.

Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu has been dropped to the bench and Manie Libbok omitted from the matchday 23 as double World Cup winner Pollard forms a new half-back pairing with Cobus Reinach. Ethan Hooker replaces the injured Cheslin Kolbe on the wing.

"Handré has delivered for us under extreme pressure," Erasmus said of Pollard, who kicked South Africa to World Cup glory in 2019 and 2023.

The bench includes Deon Fourie, Thomas du Toit, Lood de Jager, Cameron Hanekom and Morne van den Berg. Fourie could become South Africa's oldest Test player at 39 if he features, surpassing Victor Matfield and Schalk Brits.

South Africa: 15 Damian Willemse, 14 Kurt-Lee Arendse, 13 Jesse Kriel, 12 Damian de Allende, 11 Ethan Hooker, 10 Handre Pollard, 9 Cobus Reinach; 1 Ox Nche, 2 Malcolm Marx, 3 Wilco Louw, 4 Eben Etzebeth, 5 Ruan Nortje, 6 Siya Kolisi/Paul de Villiers, 7 Pieter-Steph du Toit, 8 Jasper Wiese.

articles.title: New Zealand's tour of South Africa: All Blacks come from behind to beat Lions 41-35 after huge scare in tour match
articles.summary: New Zealand fight back from 18 points down to beat the Lions and remain unbeaten on their tour of South Africa, who they beat in the first Test of their three-match series - watch the second Test live on Sky Sports Action and Sky Sports + from 4.55pm on Saturday
articles.body:
It means that the All Blacks have swept all four provincial teams to remain undefeated on their six-week, eight-match tour of South Africa, on top of beating the Springboks 33-16 in ​the first Test at the weekend.

New Zealand fielded only three players from that Saturday Test victory over South Africa on the same ground and involved five injury replacements summoned on tour - including one who arrived on Monday - as well as giving a debut to prop Saula Ma'u.

Their defence struggled and missed 19 tackles over the course of the contest that saw them trail 14-0 after seven minutes.

They were still behind at half-time and 35-17 behind in the 47th minute, as the Lions threatened to become the first South African provincial side to beat New Zealand since Orange Free State, now known as the Cheetahs, in 1976.

But like the Stormers, Sharks and Bulls who the All Blacks had already beaten, the Lions are out of season and not match fit.

Having not played since May 30 in the United Rugby Championship quarter-finals, New Zealand eventually came storming back in the last 30 minutes with four successive tries.

Rieko Ioane scored two of them, flanker Ethan Blackadder went over for a second time to earn the All Blacks the lead for the first time in the 62nd minute, while a second too by winger Emoni Narawa in the 79th finally settled the touring side's nerves.

"The Lions came out hissing," Blackadder said. "But we stayed composed and found a way in the end. They were quality tonight."

Blackadder - whose father Todd was on the last traditional tour in 1996 - was one of the New Zealand standouts along with inside center Timoci Tavatavanawai, Narawa, and fly-half Richie Mo'unga, back from Japan and in a black jersey for the first time since the 2023 World Cup final.

All Blacks coach Dave Rennie thought Blackadder was phenomenal. "He's got a massive engine and was everywhere," he said.

Blackadder's Test prospects also improved after Anton Segner was ruled out of the rest of the tour.

Segner was a late withdrawal from the first Test reserves due to an ankle injury that's needed two surgeries. The injury was assessed as acute inflammatory arthritis and he won't be replaced in the squad.

Mo'unga, like New Zealand, got better as the game got older, but he and Beauden Barrett could convert only three of the team's seven tries.

On the other hand, Chris Smith, at home, converted all five of the Lions tries and hit the post with a long penalty.
